name: Neo-grotesque sans
summary: The neutral sans of the grid: even widths, horizontal terminals, closed apertures, a large x-height and almost no contrast. It lets the layout speak and is the default voice of interfaces and corporate systems.

philosophy.core_thesis: A typeface is a neutral vessel: it carries the message and adds nothing of its own.
design_principles: Keep the stroke contrast at 1.0–1.4:1, measured on the o.
Cut the terminals of c, e, s and a horizontal, so the apertures close.
Even the widths: the capitals are close to one width, and the round letters are wide.
Hold the x-height at 0.70–0.78 of the cap height.
Use a single-storey g and a two-storey a; the R has a vertical or curved leg.
Track tighter as the size grows: 0 em at 16 px, −0.02 em at 48 px, −0.03 em above 96 px.
anti_patterns: Wide positive tracking on lower-case headlines
Mixing more than two families with it

classification.note: The neo-grotesque is a grotesque made even: horizontal terminals, uniform widths, less contrast. Some lists call it Realist.

anatomy.contrast: Almost none: the thin parts are 0.75–1.0 of the stem.
anatomy.serifs: None: the strokes end clean, with no serif.
anatomy.terminals: Horizontal on c, e, s, a and t.
anatomy.aperture: Closed: the ends of c, e and s turn in toward each other.
anatomy.key_letters: A two-storey a with a curved tail, a single-storey g, an R with a vertical leg, and a square-ish dot on i.

metrics.x_height: The x-height is 0.70–0.78 of the cap height and about 0.50–0.55 of the em.
metrics.contrast: The side of the o is 1.0 to 1.4 times as thick as its top.
metrics.width: Even widths; the mean advance of a to z is 0.50–0.56 em.
metrics.figures: Lining figures; tabular figures (tnum) for tables and interfaces.

setting.text_sizes: Set text at 9–11 pt in print and 14–17 px on screen; the large x-height allows the smaller sizes.
setting.display_sizes: Set titles at 32–160 px in medium to bold weights.
setting.leading: Set the leading at 1.4–1.55 for text, 1.1–1.2 for subheads and 0.95–1.05 for large titles.
setting.tracking: Set 0 em at 16 px, −0.01 to −0.02 em at 24–48 px, −0.03 em above 96 px, and +0.06 em for capitals.
setting.measure: Set 50–75 characters a line; a grid column sets the measure.
setting.case_and_features: Use tabular figures in tables, contextual alternates where the family has them, and the slashed zero for code.

pairing.rule: Use one family alone, in two or three weights; if you add a second face, make it a clear contrast.

pairs.why: Both have a vertical, rational build, so the page stays in one order.

pairs.role: serif for a few large titles
pairs.why: The high contrast gives the neutral page one point of drama.

reference_faces.note: Inter is not a copy of Helvetica; it is an open neo-grotesque drawn for screens, with a tall x-height (about 0.75).

negative: wide letter spacing on lower case

emotion.target_response: Order and neutrality: the reader feels a clear system and no personal voice.

avoid_when: The brand needs warmth or a personal voice.
Small text must read well for readers with low vision; a humanist sans with open apertures reads better.

modifiers.how: Open the apertures, angle the terminals, and add a little stroke modulation; keep the x-height.
Bring back the uneven widths, the spurred G and some contrast in the joins.

width.note: Univers spans condensed to extended cuts in one system.

x_height_ratio.note: Helvetica is about 0.52 and Inter about 0.55.

sources.title: Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (Hartley & Marks, 4th ed. 2012)
